meaning: Ready to work at any time if you are needed.
japanese: 呼び出しに備えて、待機している。
cue: A doctor explains why she is not drinking at dinner.
reply: I'm on call tonight, so I'll stick to water.
replyJapanese: 今夜は呼び出し待機の当番なので、水にしておきます。
transferCue: An engineer describes the weekend rota.
transferReply: Our team takes turns being on call at weekends.
transferReplyJapanese: 私たちのチームは、週末の待機当番を交代で担当しています。
nuance: No article: on call. On a call is different and means busy on the phone. Used for doctors, engineers and others who must come in if needed.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで on call。on a call は「電話中」という別の意味。必要なときに駆けつける医師や技術者などに使う。

meaning: At any time that someone wants or asks for it.
japanese: 求められたときに、いつでも。
cue: Explain how you can watch a series you missed.
reply: All the episodes are available on demand now.
replyJapanese: 今は全話、好きなときにいつでも見られます。
transferCue: A small publisher explains how it avoids waste.
transferReply: We print each book on demand, so nothing is wasted.
transferReplyJapanese: 本は注文を受けてから1冊ずつ印刷するので、無駄が出ません。
nuance: No article. Before a noun it is written with a hyphen: an on-demand service. Common for streaming and for anything supplied only when asked for.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞は付かない。名詞の前ではハイフンを入れて an on-demand service と書く。動画配信や、注文を受けてから提供するものによく使う。

meaning: Refusing to work as a protest, usually about pay or conditions.
japanese: ストライキ中である。
cue: Explain why there are no trains this morning.
reply: The drivers are on strike until Thursday.
replyJapanese: 運転士は木曜日までストライキ中です。
transferCue: Describe what happened after pay talks failed.
transferReply: The factory workers went on strike for two weeks.
transferReplyJapanese: 工場の従業員は、2週間ストライキを行いました。
frame: Be on strike / go on strike
nuance: No article: on strike, not on a strike. Go on strike is the start and be on strike is the state; the reason follows over, as in on strike over pay.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで on strike。on a strike とは言わない。go on strike は開始、be on strike は状態を表し、理由は on strike over pay のように over で示す。

meaning: Crazy, or behaving in a very foolish way.
japanese: 正気ではない。どうかしている。
cue: A friend plans to drive home through heavy snow.
reply: You must be out of your mind to drive tonight.
replyJapanese: 今夜運転するなんて、どうかしてるよ。
transferCue: Explain why you accepted a generous job offer.
transferReply: I'd be out of my mind to turn it down.
transferReplyJapanese: あれを断るとしたら、どうかしていますよ。
nuance: Informal and strong, so keep it for people you know well. The possessive changes with the person: out of my mind, out of his mind.
nuanceJapanese: くだけた強い表現なので、親しい相手に使う。所有格は人に合わせて out of my mind、out of his mind のように変わる。

meaning: Used to show that your words are not meant exactly as stated.
japanese: いわば。言ってみれば。
cue: Describe a colleague who looks after everyone in the office.
reply: She's the mother of the team, so to speak.
replyJapanese: 彼女は、いわばチームのお母さんです。
transferCue: Tell a visitor why the old printer is in a cupboard.
transferReply: That printer has retired, so to speak.
transferReplyJapanese: あのプリンターは、言ってみれば引退したんです。
nuance: Usually placed at the end after a comma, to mark a figure of speech or a playful word choice. As it were is a more formal equivalent.
nuanceJapanese: ふつう文末にコンマを置いて添え、比喩やおどけた言い回しであることを示す。as it were はより改まった同義表現。

meaning: Not value something because you expect it always to be there.
japanese: あって当たり前だと思う。ありがたみを忘れる。
cue: A power cut makes you think about daily comforts.
reply: We take electricity for granted until it goes off.
replyJapanese: 電気は、止まるまで当たり前にあるものだと思ってしまいます。
transferCue: A friend never thanks her partner for cooking.
transferReply: I think she takes him for granted these days.
transferReplyJapanese: 最近の彼女は、彼がいて当たり前だと思っている気がします。
nuance: The object goes between take and for; with a person it means not showing thanks. Take it for granted that… is another use, meaning assume without checking.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語は take と for のあいだに置く。人が目的語なら、感謝を示さないという意味。take it for granted that… は「確かめずに当然と思い込む」という別の用法。

meaning: Consider something when you judge or decide.
japanese: 考慮に入れる。
cue: Plan when to leave for the airport on a Friday.
reply: We should take the Friday traffic into account.
replyJapanese: 金曜日の渋滞を考慮に入れたほうがいいですね。
transferCue: A manager explains how a deadline was set.
transferReply: Her illness was taken into account when we set the deadline.
transferReplyJapanese: 締め切りを決める際、彼女の体調不良も考慮されました。
nuance: A short object goes in the middle; a long one can come after account. Take account of something means the same and is slightly more formal.
nuanceJapanese: 短い目的語は中に置き、長い目的語は account のあとに回せる。take account of something も同じ意味で、やや改まった言い方。

meaning: Be the first to act, especially to solve a problem.
japanese: 率先して動く。自分から行動を起こす。
cue: Nobody had organised a leaving party for a colleague.
reply: Maria took the initiative and booked a table for twenty.
replyJapanese: マリアが率先して、20人分の席を予約しました。
transferCue: Give advice to a new employee.
transferReply: Managers notice people who take the initiative in meetings.
transferReplyJapanese: 上司は、会議で自分から動く人に目を留めます。
nuance: Always with the. Use your initiative is different: it means act on your own judgement without being told what to do.
nuanceJapanese: 必ず the を付ける。use your initiative は別の表現で、指示を待たずに自分の判断で動くこと。

meaning: Used to say that the result will only be known in the future.
japanese: 時がたてば分かる。
cue: A friend asks whether your new café will succeed.
reply: Only time will tell whether the café makes money.
replyJapanese: カフェが利益を出せるかどうかは、時間がたたないと分かりません。
transferCue: Give your opinion of a team's new coach.
transferReply: He seems good so far, but time will tell.
transferReplyJapanese: 今のところ良さそうですが、いずれ分かるでしょう。
nuance: A fixed sentence: always will, and no article before time. It often follows only or but, and whether or if introduces the open question.
nuanceJapanese: 形の決まった文で、必ず will を使い、time に冠詞は付かない。only や but のあとに置くことが多く、whether や if で未確定の事柄を続ける。

meaning: Used to show that something is really stronger or worse than your words suggest.
japanese: 控えめに言っても。
cue: Describe a meeting where two managers argued.
reply: The atmosphere was tense, to say the least.
replyJapanese: 控えめに言っても、雰囲気は張り詰めていました。
transferCue: React to a hotel room that was dirty and noisy.
transferReply: We were disappointed with the room, to say the least.
transferReplyJapanese: あの部屋には、控えめに言ってもがっかりしました。
nuance: Added after a comma at the end of a statement, usually after a mild word for something bad. The article is the: never to say at least.
nuanceJapanese: 文末にコンマを置いて添える。悪い事柄を穏やかな語で述べたあとに使うことが多い。冠詞は the で、to say at least とは言わない。

meaning: Start to improve after a difficult period.
japanese: 苦しい時期を抜けて、上向き始める。峠を越す。
cue: A shop owner talks about sales after a bad year.
reply: I think the business has finally turned the corner.
replyJapanese: 店の経営は、ようやく峠を越えたと思います。
transferCue: Give news about a relative in hospital.
transferReply: The doctors say he turned the corner last night.
transferReplyJapanese: 医師によると、彼は昨夜、峠を越したそうです。
nuance: Always the corner, with no object after it. Used about an illness, a business or an economy; the literal meaning is going round the corner of a street.
nuanceJapanese: 必ず the corner で、あとに目的語は続かない。病気や事業、景気について使う。文字どおりには道の角を曲がること。

meaning: Refuse to help or support someone who needs you.
japanese: 見捨てる。背を向ける。
cue: A friend stayed loyal when you lost your job.
reply: She never turned her back on me when things got hard.
replyJapanese: 状況が厳しくなっても、彼女は決して私を見捨てませんでした。
transferCue: Explain why you will help a former boss.
transferReply: I can't turn my back on someone who trained me.
transferReplyJapanese: 自分を育ててくれた人を、見捨てることはできません。
nuance: The possessive matches the subject: turn my back on, turned her back on. With a thing as object, such as a career, it means give it up completely.
nuanceJapanese: 所有格は主語に合わせて turn my back on、turned her back on のように変える。career など物事が目的語なら、きっぱり手を引くという意味になる。

meaning: Believing something, often when it is not true.
japanese: 〜だと思い込んでいる。
cue: You arrive for a meeting on the wrong day.
reply: I was under the impression that we were meeting today.
replyJapanese: 打ち合わせは今日だと思い込んでいました。
transferCue: A hotel guest is surprised by a charge on the bill.
transferReply: He was under the impression that breakfast was included.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼は、朝食が料金に含まれていると思っていました。
nuance: The preposition is under, not in, and a that clause follows. Mostly in the past, as a polite way to admit or point out a misunderstanding.
nuanceJapanese: 前置詞は in ではなく under で、あとに that 節を続ける。主に過去形で使い、勘違いを認めたり指摘したりする丁寧な言い方になる。

meaning: Very quietly, so that other people cannot hear the words.
japanese: 聞こえないほどの小声で。
cue: A colleague reacted quietly to bad news in a meeting.
reply: He said something rude under his breath.
replyJapanese: 彼は小声で、何か失礼なことを言いました。
transferCue: Describe how you calm down before giving a speech.
transferReply: I counted to ten under my breath before I stood up.
transferReplyJapanese: 立ち上がる前に、小声で10まで数えました。
nuance: The possessive matches the speaker: under his breath, under my breath. It usually follows say, mutter or whisper, and often suggests annoyance.
nuanceJapanese: 所有格は話し手に合わせて under his breath、under my breath のように変える。say、mutter、whisper のあとに置くことが多く、不満の含みを持ちやすい。

meaning: The damage that happens to something through ordinary use.
japanese: 普通に使ううちに生じる傷み。消耗。
cue: A tenant asks about marks on the carpet.
reply: The landlord can't charge you for normal wear and tear.
replyJapanese: 通常の使用による傷みについては、大家は費用を請求できません。
transferCue: Explain why you are replacing an old sofa.
transferReply: The sofa shows ten years of wear and tear.
transferReplyJapanese: ソファには、10年分の傷みが出ています。
nuance: Uncountable: no a and no plural, and the word order never changes. This tear rhymes with hair, not with ear.
nuanceJapanese: 不可算で、a も複数形も付かず、語順も変わらない。この tear は ear ではなく hair と同じ韻で発音する。

meaning: Be a particular total when amounts are added together.
japanese: 合計で、〜になる。
cue: Tell a friend how much dinner for four cost.
reply: The bill came to ninety pounds with the tip.
replyJapanese: お会計は、チップ込みで90ポンドになりました。
transferCue: A mechanic adds up the cost of a repair.
transferReply: The parts and labour come to about three hundred euros.
transferReplyJapanese: 部品代と作業費で、合計約300ユーロになります。
nuance: Inseparable, and not used in the passive or the continuous in this sense. The subject is the bill or the costs, and the amount follows directly.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。この意味では受け身や進行形にしない。主語は請求額や費用で、金額を直後に続ける。
contrast: Come to states the final total; add up to stresses the adding of several separate amounts.
contrastJapanese: come to は最終的な合計を述べる。add up to はいくつもの金額を足していく点に重点がある。

meaning: Start doing something without planning to.
japanese: なりゆきで、何かを始める。
cue: Explain how your career began.
reply: I fell into teaching by accident after university.
replyJapanese: 大学を出たあと、たまたま教える仕事に就きました。
transferCue: Describe a bad routine during a busy month.
transferReply: We fell into the habit of eating dinner at ten.
transferReplyJapanese: 夜10時に夕食をとる習慣が、いつの間にかついてしまいました。
nuance: Inseparable. Typical objects are a habit, a routine, a job and conversation. It suggests chance, not a plan.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。目的語は a habit、a routine、a job、conversation などが典型的。計画ではなく、なりゆきという含みがある。
contrast: Fall into happens without a plan; take up is a deliberate decision to start a hobby or a job.
contrastJapanese: fall into は計画なしに始まること。take up は趣味や仕事を自分の意志で始めること。

meaning: Listen to someone until they have finished speaking.
japanese: 話を最後まで聞く。
cue: A colleague interrupts your idea halfway through.
reply: Please hear me out before you say no.
replyJapanese: 断る前に、最後まで話を聞いてください。
transferCue: Describe a fair manager.
transferReply: She heard everyone out and then made her decision.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は全員の話を最後まで聞いてから、決断しました。
nuance: Separable, and the person always goes in the middle: hear me out, not hear out me. Often a request when you expect to be interrupted.
nuanceJapanese: 分離でき、人は必ず中に置く。hear me out と言い、hear out me とは言わない。話を遮られそうなときの頼みとして使うことが多い。
contrast: Hear out means listening right to the end; listen to says nothing about letting the person finish.
contrastJapanese: hear out は最後まで聞くこと。listen to には、相手に話し終えさせるという含みはない。

meaning: Come before an event and continue until it begins.
japanese: ある出来事に至るまで続く。
cue: Describe how busy a shop gets in December.
reply: The weeks leading up to Christmas are always hectic.
replyJapanese: クリスマスまでの数週間は、いつも大忙しです。
transferCue: A reporter explains why a factory closed.
transferReply: Nobody noticed the events that led up to the closure.
transferReplyJapanese: 閉鎖に至るまでの出来事に、誰も気づいていませんでした。
nuance: Inseparable. Very common as leading up to after a time word: the days leading up to the exam. The noun is the lead-up to something.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。the days leading up to the exam のように、時を表す語のあとで leading up to の形でよく使う。名詞は the lead-up to something。
contrast: Lead up to covers the time before an event; lead to means cause a result.
contrastJapanese: lead up to は出来事の前の期間を表す。lead to は結果を引き起こすこと。

meaning: Be going to happen in the future.
japanese: この先に待ち受けている。
cue: Speak to students on their last day of school.
reply: Exciting challenges lie ahead for all of you.
replyJapanese: 皆さんの前には、わくわくするような挑戦が待っています。
transferCue: A manager warns the team after a poor quarter.
transferReply: A difficult few months lie ahead of us.
transferReplyJapanese: これから数か月、厳しい時期が私たちを待ち受けています。
frame: Lie ahead of someone / for someone
nuance: No object. The past form is lay ahead, not lied ahead. The person follows for or of: what lies ahead for us.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語は取らない。過去形は lay ahead で、lied ahead とは言わない。人は what lies ahead for us のように for か of で続ける。
contrast: Lie ahead simply says something is coming; be in store suggests it is waiting for one particular person.
contrastJapanese: lie ahead は単にこの先にあると述べる。be in store は特定の人を待ち受けているという含みがある。

meaning: Accept a difficult or unpleasant situation that continues.
japanese: 嫌な状況を、受け入れてやっていく。
cue: Your flat is next to a busy road.
reply: The noise is annoying, but I can live with it.
replyJapanese: 騒音は気になりますが、我慢できる範囲です。
transferCue: Talk about a relative with an old injury.
transferReply: She has learned to live with the pain in her knee.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は、膝の痛みとうまく付き合えるようになりました。
nuance: Inseparable. Common after can, have to and learn to. I can live with that is a usual way to accept a compromise.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。can、have to、learn to のあとでよく使う。I can live with that は、妥協案を受け入れるときの決まった言い方。
contrast: Live with means accepting something that will not change; put up with stresses your patience with something annoying.
contrastJapanese: live with は変わらないものを受け入れること。put up with は嫌なことを我慢する点に重点がある。

meaning: Not get something good that you wanted or that others get.
japanese: 得られるはずのものを逃す。損をする。
cue: You booked concert tickets a day too late.
reply: We lost out on the cheap seats by one day.
replyJapanese: 1日の差で、安い席を取り損ねました。
transferCue: Explain who is affected when a bus route closes.
transferReply: Older residents will lose out if the route closes.
transferReplyJapanese: その路線が廃止されれば、高齢の住民が不利益を受けます。
frame: Lose out on something / lose out to someone
nuance: No direct object: on introduces the thing you miss, and to introduces the person who gets it instead. The past form is lost out.
nuanceJapanese: 直接目的語は取らない。逃すものは on、代わりに得る相手は to で示す。過去形は lost out。
contrast: Lose out means failing to get a benefit, often unfairly; miss out means not taking part in something enjoyable.
contrastJapanese: lose out は利益を得られないことで、不公平だという含みを持ちやすい。miss out は楽しいことに加われないこと。

meaning: Choose one thing instead of the others.
japanese: いくつかの中から、〜を選ぶ。
cue: Explain your choice at a car showroom.
reply: We opted for the smaller model to save fuel.
replyJapanese: 燃料を節約するために、小さいほうのモデルを選びました。
transferCue: Describe what guests chose at a wedding dinner.
transferReply: Most guests opted for the fish instead of the beef.
transferReplyJapanese: ほとんどの招待客が、牛肉ではなく魚を選びました。
nuance: Inseparable and slightly formal. Before a verb, drop for and use opt to: we opted to stay.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できず、やや改まった表現。動詞を続けるときは for を使わず、we opted to stay のように opt to とする。
contrast: Opt for is a considered choice between options; go for is the casual, everyday way to say it.
contrastJapanese: opt for は選択肢をよく比べて選ぶこと。go for は同じ内容のくだけた日常的な言い方。

meaning: Notice something that other people have not noticed.
japanese: ほかの人が気づかないことに、気づく。
cue: A friend noticed you were upset at a party.
reply: Only Anna picked up on how quiet I was.
replyJapanese: 私の口数が少ないことに気づいたのは、アンナだけでした。
transferCue: Praise a careful proofreader.
transferReply: He picked up on two mistakes that everyone else missed.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼は、ほかの誰もが見逃した2つの間違いに気づきました。
nuance: Inseparable: the object comes after on. Used for small signs such as a mood, a hint or a detail.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できず、目的語は on のあとに置く。気分、ほのめかし、細部といった小さな兆しに使う。
contrast: Pick up on means noticing something subtle; pick up means learning or collecting something.
contrastJapanese: pick up on は微妙な点に気づくこと。pick up は身につけたり、受け取ったりすること。

meaning: Tell someone what to do in a rude or threatening way.
japanese: 偉そうに、あれこれ指図する。こき使う。
cue: A new employee keeps getting orders from an older colleague.
reply: Don't let him push you around because you're new.
replyJapanese: 新人だからといって、彼の言いなりになってはいけません。
transferCue: Explain why you finally argued with your brother.
transferReply: I was tired of being pushed around by my brother.
transferReplyJapanese: 兄にあれこれ指図されるのは、もううんざりでした。
nuance: Separable, with the person in the middle. British English also says push about. Common in the passive: be pushed around.
nuanceJapanese: 分離でき、人を中に置く。イギリス英語では push about とも言う。be pushed around と受け身でよく使う。
contrast: Push around means giving rude, threatening orders; boss around is milder and suggests an annoying habit.
contrastJapanese: push around は威圧的で無礼な指図をすること。boss around はもっと軽く、うっとうしい癖という含みがある。

meaning: Control someone so strongly that they stop thinking clearly.
japanese: 感情や想像が、抑えられなくなる。
cue: A friend imagines the worst after one late reply.
reply: You're letting your imagination run away with you again.
replyJapanese: また想像ばかりが先走っているよ。
transferCue: Apologise for speaking too long in a meeting.
transferReply: Sorry, my enthusiasm ran away with me there.
transferReplyJapanese: すみません、つい熱が入りすぎてしまいました。
frame: Let something run away with you
nuance: The feeling is the subject and the person follows with: my temper ran away with me. Most common with imagination, after let.
nuanceJapanese: 感情が主語になり、人は with のあとに置く。例は my temper ran away with me。let のあとで imagination とともに使うことが最も多い。
contrast: Run away with makes the feeling the subject; get carried away makes the person the subject.
contrastJapanese: run away with は感情を主語にする。get carried away は人を主語にする。

meaning: End a letter, message or broadcast with some final words.
japanese: 手紙や放送を、結びの言葉で締めくくる。
cue: Explain how you end emails to clients.
reply: I usually sign off with a simple thank you.
replyJapanese: 私はたいてい、簡単なお礼の言葉で締めくくります。
transferCue: Describe the end of a late-night radio show.
transferReply: The presenter signed off with a song for night workers.
transferReplyJapanese: 司会者は、夜勤で働く人たちに1曲贈って番組を締めくくりました。
nuance: Usually has no object; with introduces the closing words. Sign off on a plan is a different use, meaning approve it.
nuanceJapanese: ふつう目的語は取らず、結びの言葉は with で示す。sign off on a plan は別の用法で、計画を承認するという意味。
contrast: Sign off closes a letter or programme with final words; sign out records that you are leaving a building or an account.
contrastJapanese: sign off は手紙や番組を結びの言葉で終えること。sign out は建物やアカウントから出る記録を残すこと。

meaning: Avoid reading or looking at a part of something.
japanese: ある部分を、読まずに飛ばす。
cue: Admit that you did not read all of a long contract.
reply: I skipped over the pages about insurance.
replyJapanese: 保険に関するページは読み飛ばしました。
transferCue: Give advice on reading a difficult novel.
transferReply: You can skip over the long descriptions in chapter two.
transferReplyJapanese: 第2章の長い描写は、読み飛ばしてかまいません。
nuance: Inseparable. Skip alone means the same and is more common in speech; over adds the picture of jumping across a part to reach the next.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。skip だけでも同じ意味で、会話ではそのほうが多い。over が付くと、ある部分を飛び越えて次へ進むイメージが加わる。
contrast: Skip over leaves a part unread; skim through reads all of it quickly without detail.
contrastJapanese: skip over はある部分を読まずに飛ばす。skim through は全体をざっと速く読む。

meaning: Leave quietly so that nobody notices.
japanese: 気づかれないように、そっと立ち去る。
cue: You left a party early without saying goodbye.
reply: I slipped away while everyone was dancing.
replyJapanese: みんなが踊っているあいだに、そっと抜け出しました。
transferCue: Suggest leaving a long reception early.
transferReply: Let's slip away after the speeches and get some dinner.
transferReplyJapanese: スピーチが終わったら、こっそり抜けて夕食を食べに行こう。
nuance: No object; from introduces the place. The aim is to avoid attention, not to escape from danger.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語は取らず、場所は from で示す。危険から逃げるのではなく、人目を引かずに出るのが目的。
contrast: Slip away means leaving unnoticed; sneak off is more informal and suggests you are not supposed to leave.
contrastJapanese: slip away は気づかれずに立ち去ること。sneak off はよりくだけた言い方で、本来は抜けてはいけないという含みがある。

meaning: Be said by accident, without the speaker intending it.
japanese: うっかり口から出る。
cue: You accidentally revealed a surprise party.
reply: I'm sorry, the secret just slipped out.
replyJapanese: ごめんなさい、秘密をうっかり口にしてしまいました。
transferCue: Explain how a colleague learned about your new job.
transferReply: It slipped out while we were chatting over lunch.
transferReplyJapanese: 昼食をとりながら話していて、つい口が滑りました。
nuance: The remark or secret is the subject, not the speaker: it slipped out. Just often comes before it to show there was no intention.
nuanceJapanese: 主語は話し手ではなく、発言や秘密のほうで、it slipped out と言う。just を前に置いて、わざとではないことを示すことが多い。
contrast: Slip out makes the words the subject and the mistake a quiet one; blurt out has the speaker saying something suddenly.
contrastJapanese: slip out は言葉が主語で、静かにうっかり漏れること。blurt out は話し手が主語で、突然口走ること。

meaning: Cause a problem or a bad feeling to begin or grow.
japanese: もめ事や悪い感情を、かき立てる。
cue: A colleague keeps repeating gossip to two teams.
reply: He's just trying to stir up trouble between the teams.
replyJapanese: 彼は、チーム同士のあいだにもめ事を起こそうとしているだけです。
transferCue: Describe the effect of a newspaper report.
transferReply: The article stirred up a lot of anger in the town.
transferReplyJapanese: その記事は、町じゅうに大きな怒りをかき立てました。
frame: Stir up something / stir something up
nuance: Separable, and a pronoun must go in the middle: stir it up. The object is usually negative, such as trouble, anger or fear.
nuanceJapanese: 分離でき、代名詞は必ず中に置いて stir it up とする。目的語は trouble、anger、fear など、たいてい否定的なもの。
contrast: Stir up usually creates trouble or bad feeling; whip up can also raise good things such as excitement or support.
contrastJapanese: stir up はふつう、もめ事や悪い感情を生む。whip up は興奮や支持など、良いものをかき立てるときにも使う。

meaning: Leave a place in a way that shows you are angry.
japanese: 怒って、その場を飛び出す。
cue: Describe how an argument at dinner ended.
reply: He stormed out before dessert and slammed the door.
replyJapanese: 彼はデザートの前に怒って出て行き、ドアを乱暴に閉めました。
transferCue: A colleague read an email about budget cuts.
transferReply: She stormed out of the office after reading the email.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女はそのメールを読むと、怒ってオフィスを飛び出しました。
nuance: No object; of introduces the place: storm out of the room. The anger is plain to see and usually noisy.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語は取らず、場所は of で示して storm out of the room とする。怒りがはっきり見て取れ、たいてい音も荒い。
contrast: Storm out shows anger in the moment; walk out can be a calm, deliberate protest.
contrastJapanese: storm out はその場の怒りをあらわにする。walk out は落ち着いた、意図的な抗議にもなる。

meaning: Treat someone badly because you are upset, though they did nothing wrong.
japanese: 八つ当たりする。
cue: A friend snaps at you after a bad day at work.
reply: I know you're stressed, but don't take it out on me.
replyJapanese: ストレスがたまっているのは分かるけど、私に当たらないで。
transferCue: Apologise to your family after a hard week.
transferReply: I'm sorry I took my bad mood out on you all.
transferReplyJapanese: 機嫌が悪くて、みんなに当たってしまってごめんなさい。
nuance: The feeling goes between take and out, and the person comes after on. Take it out on someone is the most common form, where it means the anger.
nuanceJapanese: 感情は take と out のあいだに、相手は on のあとに置く。take it out on someone の形が最も多く、it は怒りを指す。
contrast: Take out on means making an innocent person suffer for your mood; lash out at means suddenly attacking someone in anger.
contrastJapanese: take out on は罪のない人に不機嫌をぶつけること。lash out at は怒りにまかせて突然相手を攻撃すること。

meaning: Start to like someone or something.
japanese: 好きになる。なじむ。
cue: Your shy cat met the new neighbour.
reply: The cat took to our neighbour straight away.
replyJapanese: うちの猫は、すぐにお隣さんになつきました。
transferCue: Describe a child's first swimming lessons.
transferReply: She took to swimming much faster than we expected.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は、私たちが思っていたよりずっと早く水泳になじみました。
nuance: Inseparable. Often with an adverb of speed such as immediately or straight away. In the negative it means fail to warm to someone.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できない。immediately や straight away など、速さを表す副詞を伴うことが多い。否定形では、相手に好感を持てないという意味になる。
contrast: Take to means starting to like something new; take up means starting an activity, whether you enjoy it or not.
contrastJapanese: take to は新しいものを好きになること。take up は楽しいかどうかに関係なく、活動を始めること。

meaning: Improve something by making small changes.
japanese: 少し手を加えて、仕上げ直す。手直しする。
cue: A wall has a few marks before guests arrive.
reply: I'll touch up the paint in the hall before Saturday.
replyJapanese: 土曜日までに、玄関ホールの塗装を手直ししておきます。
transferCue: A photographer explains what happens after a shoot.
transferReply: We touch the photos up before sending them to clients.
transferReplyJapanese: 写真は、手直ししてからお客様に送ります。
frame: Touch something up / touch up something
nuance: Separable. Used for paint, make-up, photos and writing, always for small improvements. Keep the object a thing: with a person as object it has a rude meaning in British English.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できる。塗装、化粧、写真、文章などの小さな手直しに使う。目的語は物に限ること。人を目的語にすると、イギリス英語では下品な意味になる。
contrast: Touch up makes small improvements to something finished; do up repairs or decorates it completely.
contrastJapanese: touch up は仕上がったものに小さな手直しをする。do up は全面的に修理や改装をする。

meaning: Lead to something as a result.
japanese: 結果として、〜につながる。
cue: A manager questions whether website traffic matters.
reply: More visitors don't always translate into more sales.
replyJapanese: 訪問者が増えても、売上が増えるとは限りません。
transferCue: Comment on a candidate who was famous online.
transferReply: Her popularity online didn't translate into votes on election day.
transferReplyJapanese: ネットでの人気は、投票日の得票にはつながりませんでした。
nuance: Inseparable, with the result after into. Common in the negative, to say a good sign did not produce the expected result.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できず、結果は into のあとに置く。良い兆しが期待した結果に結びつかなかったと述べる否定文でよく使う。
contrast: Translate into turns one thing into a matching result; lead to names any cause and effect.
contrastJapanese: translate into は、あるものがそれに見合う結果に変わること。lead to は因果関係全般に使う。

meaning: Start to understand that a problem or situation exists.
japanese: 問題や状況に、ようやく気づく。
cue: A town ignored flood warnings for years.
reply: The council has finally woken up to the flood risk.
replyJapanese: 市議会は、ようやく洪水の危険性に気づきました。
transferCue: Say that employers are slow to notice a change.
transferReply: Companies are waking up to the cost of losing staff.
transferReplyJapanese: 企業は、人材を失うことの代償に気づき始めています。
nuance: To is a preposition, so a noun or the fact that follows. It suggests the understanding comes late, after the signs were ignored.
nuanceJapanese: この to は前置詞なので、名詞か the fact that を続ける。兆しを見過ごしたあとで、遅れて気づくという含みがある。
contrast: Wake up to means realising a problem late; face up to means accepting a problem you already know about.
contrastJapanese: wake up to は遅れて問題に気づくこと。face up to はすでに分かっている問題を受け止めること。

meaning: Enter a room and see someone doing something private.
japanese: 人に見られたくない場面に、うっかり入ってしまう。
cue: You opened the wrong door at the office.
reply: I walked in on a private meeting by mistake.
replyJapanese: 間違えて、内輪の会議の最中に入ってしまいました。
transferCue: Explain why a birthday surprise failed.
transferReply: She walked in on us wrapping her present.
transferReplyJapanese: プレゼントを包んでいるところに、彼女が入ってきてしまいました。
nuance: Inseparable, with the person or event after on. An -ing form can follow the person: walk in on someone doing something.
nuanceJapanese: 分離できず、人や出来事は on のあとに置く。walk in on someone doing something のように、人のあとに -ing 形を続けられる。
contrast: Walk in on means entering and seeing something private by chance; barge in means entering rudely, whatever is happening inside.
contrastJapanese: walk in on は偶然入って私的な場面を見てしまうこと。barge in は中の様子に構わず、無遠慮に入ること。

meaning: Leave an event before it ends because you are angry or do not approve.
japanese: 不満や抗議を示して、途中で退席する。
cue: A film was much worse than the reviews said.
reply: Half the audience walked out before the end.
replyJapanese: 観客の半分が、終わる前に席を立ちました。
transferCue: A minister said something offensive at a conference.
transferReply: Several delegates walked out during the minister's speech.
transferReplyJapanese: 大臣の演説中に、数人の代表が退席しました。
nuance: No object; of introduces the event. Walk out on someone is a different use, meaning leave a partner or family.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語は取らず、退席する場は of で示す。walk out on someone は別の用法で、パートナーや家族を捨てて出て行くという意味。
contrast: Walk out is leaving in protest or disgust; walk away means leaving a situation you choose not to deal with.
contrastJapanese: walk out は抗議や嫌悪を示して立ち去ること。walk away は関わらないと決めて、その状況から離れること。

meaning: Deal with a problem that has many parts, step by step.
japanese: 込み入った問題を、ひとつずつ片づけていく。
cue: A long list of customer complaints needs answers.
reply: We're working through the complaints one by one.
replyJapanese: 苦情に、1件ずつ順番に対応しているところです。
transferCue: Suggest how to prepare for Friday's meeting.
transferReply: Let's work through the budget issues before Friday's meeting.
transferReplyJapanese: 金曜日の会議までに、予算の問題を順に片づけましょう。
nuance: The object usually comes after through. It suggests steady progress over time, so it suits long lists and problems with many parts.
nuanceJapanese: 目的語はふつう through のあとに置く。時間をかけて着実に進める含みがあり、長いリストや込み入った問題に合う。
contrast: Work through deals with a problem part by part; work out finds the answer or solution.
contrastJapanese: work through は問題を部分ごとに片づけていく。work out は答えや解決策を見つける。
